1: This briefing is Book 13 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, Governance, Drift and Evidence.
It's about why compliance starts to decay the day after the audit, and what governance that doesn't decay looks like.
Why does a signed package start aging at once?
What keeps governance true between assessments?
And how do you run it at machine tempo, reuse it across agencies, and scale it?
The short version: keep one authoritative record, let the systems prove they still match it, and keep people on the decisions only people can make.
The slides and notes carry every detail and source; I'll stick to what matters.
Let's start with the day the package is signed.
2: Picture the week an authorization package is signed.
On that day, the package is true.
The next morning, an administrator changes a firewall rule to fix an outage.
A contractor's account outlives the contract.
A cloud provider ships a new default.
None of it reaches the package.
Federal guidance already points away from the snapshot.
FISMA sets an annual testing floor, and there's no federal three-year rule; the term is the agency's to set.
nist and O M B both push agencies toward ongoing authorization, rather than a single point-in-time decision.
So why do so few systems get there?
nist answers that too: without substantial automation, ongoing authorization isn't practical.
And adding checkboxes makes the reporting heavier while leaving the change untouched.
Next, the name for what's going wrong.
3: The mechanism has a name: drift.
Drift is any difference between what the authoritative record says should be true and what the running estate actually does.
A setting changed and never recorded.
An account that outlived its owner.
A rule that quietly stopped evaluating.
nist names the sources, from attackers to honest mistakes, changes outside change control, provider changes, staff turnover and upgrades.
The program ranks drift first among governance threats, for three reasons.
It's continuous, a gradient rather than an event.
It's silent, because every console reports what it was told, not what's true.
And it's the opening other threats use; NSA and sis-uh call common misconfigurations systemic weaknesses.
nist's controls already describe drift detection without using the word: a baseline, controlled change, approved deviations, and someone who keeps checking.
Next, what drift is measured against.
4: Drift can only be measured against something.
For twenty years, many enterprises kept their governance, unwritten, in the Active Directory tree.
A flat cloud directory doesn't carry it, so the program writes the governance down, in one authoritative record.
That record is a version-controlled repository of policies, plans, evidence, schemas and rules.
It doesn't master every fact; HR still owns who a worker is.
What it holds is the authority: which system owns each fact, and who may write it.
Runtime systems read it and never write it.
Private copies are forbidden, because a local copy someone reads because the repository was slow is a second source of truth.
And every derived report carries its source, version, time and producer.
In nist terms, this record is the baseline, kept in a form machines can compare.
Next, how changes get into it.
5: A record is only as good as the path into it.
Most drift isn't malicious; it's a hotfix during an outage.
So the program allows one path for every operational change, and no second path for urgent work.

The path has five clauses: originate from the source of truth, authorize from the authority model, execute with just-in-time least privilege, close with verification, and emit the evidence automatically.
Skip a clause, and it's not a change with a missing form.
Changes to the record itself travel as reviewed pull requests, with two people and protections that bind administrators too.
Emergencies are back-ported within one business day, and reported as drift until then.
The identity that decides never acts, and the one that acts never decides.
And no closure counts unless it carries its proof.
6: When the program says a control is satisfied, how does anyone know it's right?
Give it the same version of the record and the same inputs, and it produces the same evidence, byte for byte.
So an assessor doesn't have to trust the run.
They repeat it and compare the hashes.
Automation makes the answer arrive faster; determinism makes it the same answer no matter who asks.

The rules live in three layers, each with its own reviewer: rules that say what things mean, mappings that say which rules apply to which controls, and runtime code, the only layer allowed to change state.
One honest limit: determinism is faithful to the record, not a check on it.
A wrong rule gives the same wrong answer every time.
7: The drift engine compares what it observes with the versioned record, not with a last-known-good snapshot.
An approved change updates the record first, so it isn't drift.
There's one drift model, with five classes, each asking one question, like whether a value is still true, or whether every change traces to an authorized source.
The drift checks in the other books are instances of these five, not separate lists.
Severity is computed, not argued, from the class and whether the claim is in active use.
The top severity halts and alerts a named role, and is never fixed automatically; the others get set response windows.
Severity sets the clock, and the actuation ladder decides who may act.
And be precise with an assessor about what's built: two classes are built, one is partial, and two are still design.
8: An attestation is a person signing that a system was in a stated condition.
It answers who is accountable, and federal authorization needs that answer.
Evidence answers a different question: is the claim true, and can I check it?
The program inverts the usual package.
Evidence is the substance, and attestation is the accountability wrapper, so people sign for the rules, the exceptions and the acceptance of risk.
nist treats automated comparison of intended and actual state as equivalent to assessment results, and fed-ramp's 2026 rules tell assessors not to simply review documentation or screenshots.
But be careful what you claim.
A hash chain shows removal or reordering.
Only a signature shows who produced it.
And some controls, like a training record or a contract clause, stay attestations.
Next, how the program reaches each platform.
9: The program doesn't replace the platforms an agency runs.
It reaches each one through an adapter: a translator that reads the platform's native state and writes it into the common record, with provenance.
The rules, the drift engine and the evidence chain see one record, whichever vendor produced it.
And adapters hold no rules and make no decisions.
There are two kinds, kept in separate lists.
Modernization adapters change state, only on authorized plans, and with an approver by default.
Read-only comes first, and it has to be verified.
ScubaGear is read-only in purpose, yet a Global Administrator always has the permissions it needs, so the program compares what an identity is granted with what it declares.
It moves to small, replaceable adapters, and to a record the agency owns.
10: None of this machinery decides anything.
A drift finding asks a question: change the estate, change the record, or carry the difference?
Only people can answer the last two, so the program names one decider for each.
The steward keeps the record, its protections and backups, but doesn't decide what the facts mean; the business owners do.
The see-so decides control requirements, even when they're written as code.
The governance board is the change control body nist calls for, and it reviews rather than votes, so every decision keeps one accountable owner.
The authorizing official, the only one who can accept risk, signs every open-ended gap and every class of change allowed to run unattended.
A bounded exception, with an end date, is the see-so's, and none renews automatically.
And because the repository is a federal record, its history is never rewritten without the records officer.
11: A platform that detects perfectly but closes slowly produces an accurate list of things nobody fixed.
The program sets a response window for each severity, and external clocks win, like the vulnerability directive or sis-uh's incident notice.
The usual ticket sends a person to a console, and their reply of done is just an assertion.
The program's rule is that wherever a machine can reach the surface, the ticket authorizes a machine.
A person approves, and the platform executes from a versioned plan, after a dry run, then re-reads the object to verify.
By default, a named approver releases each instance.
Only classes the authorizing official accepts in advance run on their own, and some, like Conditional Access, never do.
Where no machine can reach, the fallback is a declared, recorded privileged session, never a quiet trip to the console.
12: A platform that twenty agencies use gets examined by twenty assessment teams, producing twenty snapshots at twenty different times.
Reciprocity is the alternative: agencies accept each other's assessments.
But nothing in it lets one authorizing official accept risk for another agency.

nist gives mechanisms for this, like an authorization to use, where an agency accepts another's package and carries full responsibility for it, or a joint authorization, where several officials accept one system's risk together.
For cloud services, O M B makes reuse the default: agencies presume a fed-ramp package is adequate, but only while continuous monitoring maintains it.
And each agency still authorizes its own systems.
So the program corrects its old single-authorization wording.
It's one package, and many decisions, with each agency signing for its own risk.
13: A real agency doesn't have one estate.
It has hundreds of systems and several boundaries, and nist expects each system's monitoring to follow one organization-wide strategy.
The program's scaling rule is simple: hold the definitions small, and let the uses grow.
The record's core, the drift classes and the severities stay fixed, so a top-severity finding means the same thing in every program.
Adapters, mappings and evidence grow, each validated on entry.
Boundaries are recorded as governed objects, so findings cite the boundary they crossed.
Every control is covered, partial, a gap, or out of scope.
Every partial or gap goes into a register with an owner, the evidence that will prove closure, and a date.
14: Charter the governance board in writing and name the steward, with one decider for every kind of decision.
Settle the record before the next migration: which system owns each fact, the rules, and the provenance each value carries, so a migration changes who supplies a fact, not what it means.
Set the tempo: response windows by severity, an approver by default, and the authorizing official's signature on every class that runs on its own.
And plan the move to ongoing authorization, on evidence the systems produce rather than attestations people assemble.
The next step needs no procurement.
Classify every control's coverage, open the gap register, and record every drift finding in the same shape, however it was found.
Governance that doesn't decay keeps proving itself every day after.
Book 13 has the detail, every claim footnoted.
